name: Leave-in conditioner

lead: A leave-in conditioner is applied to damp hair after washing and not rinsed out. It keeps hair softer, smoother and easier to comb between washes, and the smoothing shows right away.

Light conditioning agents, usually cationic surfactants, silicones, humectants and oils, coat the fibre, flatten the cuticle, reduce friction and static, and leave a thin film until the next wash. It works on the surface, since hair cannot be repaired biologically, and no trials of the product category were found.

paras: Used as creams, lotions, sprays or mists on the lengths and ends after washing, daily or as needed. Some versions add heat or UV protection and are used before styling.
Considered a low-risk cosmetic. Buildup and scalp flaking are reported with heavy use or application at the roots, and individual ingredients can cause allergic reactions.

angle.text: Leave-in conditioner is applied after washing for daily softness, detangling and frizz control. The smoothing effect is visible right away and temporary, and some formulas add heat protection.

lead: A leave-in conditioner is a no-rinse hair product applied to damp (or sometimes dry) hair after washing and left in. People use it to make hair look smoother, shinier and more controlled through the day: less frizz and static, easier combing and styling, softer feel, definition for curls and coils, and in some formulas protection from heat tools. For anyone working on hair as part of their overall look, it is a quick way to improve how the hair lies and reflects light.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes leave-in conditioners as lighter than rinse-out types, often containing silicones or polymers that reduce static and may give some heat and UV protection.[2] Conditioners in general improve combability and appearance by reducing friction between fibres; they coat the hair rather than repair it, since the hair shaft is not living tissue.[2] Formats include creams, lotions, sprays and mists.[1]

Laboratory work on conditioning agents supports the friction-and-breakage logic. A 2026 study adapting wet-combing methods to textured hair found that tested conditioning products reduced hair friction by about 50 to 60 percent, and that conditioning and lubricating treatments reduced broken fibres by 38 to 64 percent, with silicone oil showing the largest reduction.[3] No clinical trials of leave-in conditioners as a product category were found.[2]
infobox: Cationic surfactants, silicones, humectants, oils, proteins[1][2]
Rinse-out conditioners, deep conditioners and hair masks, co-wash[2]
Temporary cosmetic effect until next wash[2]

paras: Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, lists typical ingredients as humectants such as glycerin, silicones such as dimethicone, plant oils such as argan or jojoba, proteins and vitamins.[1] Wikipedia's article on conditioners names cationic surfactants (such as cetrimonium chloride, behentrimonium chloride and stearalkonium chloride), cationic polymers such as polyquaternium-10, fatty alcohols, silicones, hydrolysed proteins, panthenol, humectants, acidifiers, sequestrants, UV filters and thermal protectants as typical components of conditioners generally.[2]

Wikipedia explains that undamaged hair has a hydrophobic lipid film on its cuticle, and that weathering, bleaching, dyeing and heat styling strip it and leave a more hydrophilic, negatively charged surface. Cationic surfactants bind to that surface with their hydrophobic tails facing outward, which flattens the cuticle scales, reduces static and flyaways and gives oils and silicones something to bond to.[2] Damaged hair carries more negative sites and so absorbs more conditioner.[2]

Other components have specific roles. Acidifiers such as citric acid keep the product acidic, which lowers the fibre's net negative charge, tightens the cuticle and reduces frizz; silicones fill cuticle defects, reduce friction and add shine, with volatile silicones leaving a lighter finish; panthenol penetrates the fibre and has been reported to raise break stress; and hydrolysed proteins of low molecular weight can enter the cortex, though the effect is temporary and removed by shampooing.[2]

Rinse-out conditioners are the most common type, applied after shampooing and rinsed after a few minutes, while leave-ins stay in the hair.[1][2] Deep conditioners or hair masks are thicker and are left on for about 20 to 30 minutes.[2] Leave-in formulas are described as lighter so they do not weigh hair down, and some products include UV filters, chelating agents for hard water or thermal-protectant polymers aimed at heat tools above 200 degrees Celsius.[1][2]

Cleansing conditioners (co-washes) replace shampoo and are used mainly on dry, sensitive, over-processed or textured hair, usually alternated with a clarifying shampoo; two-in-one conditioning shampoos are described as less effective than dedicated conditioners because anionic detergents and cationic agents can form complexes.[2]

For straight and wavy hair, leave-ins are used to smooth the surface, cut frizz and static, add shine and make hair easier to comb and style. For curly and textured hair they are used to keep curls defined and flexible and to reduce breakage during detangling and styling. A 2026 set of method papers on textured hair describes tests for combing force, shine, curl shrinkage, flexibility and consumer-perceived porosity, and reports that effective shine treatments improved shine and restored colour vibrancy, while some gels increased curl stiffness and other products kept flexibility close to that of virgin hair.[3][3]

Single-fibre fatigue experiments on textured hair indicate that it can break far more under repeated stress than standard tensile tests suggest, and that higher grooming forces make breakage accelerate steeply, which is the rationale for lubricating products used before combing.[3] In the combing study, natural oils did not reduce friction but did reduce combing breakage.[3]

Where hair is heat-styled, Wikipedia notes that thermal-protectant polymers form films that shield hair from blow-dryers and irons that can exceed 200 degrees Celsius, and cites a 2011 study in which pretreatment with certain polymers reduced breakage on combing and limited thermal damage to keratin.[2]

Wikipedia notes that people have used natural oils on hair for centuries. Macassar oil, a scented dressing sold from the 1790s by London barber Alexander Rowland, was widely used by men through much of the 19th century, and its greasy residue led to washable antimacassar covers around 1850.[2] Modern conditioner is commonly dated to about 1900, when Edouard Pinaud presented Brilliantine at the Paris Exposition, a claim the article flags as uncited. Silicones, fatty alcohols, quaternary ammonium compounds and polymers later replaced simple oils.[2]

Manufacturers and secondary sources describe less frizz, easier combing, reduced breakage, added shine and some protection from heat styling.[1] Wikipedia notes that benefits such as repair and strengthening are often advertised but are not treated as established, because the hair shaft is dead tissue that cannot regenerate biologically.[2] Laboratory studies it cites include reduced combing breakage after certain polymer pretreatments before hot flat-ironing and increased break stress with panthenol in one study.[2]

Product guidance summarised by Grokipedia advises applying leave-ins to mid-lengths and ends and avoiding the scalp to prevent buildup or irritation, and says dermatologists recommend washing out accumulated residue periodically.[1] Wikipedia notes that conditioner left on the scalp can dry and flake in a way that resembles dandruff.

Epidemiological and chemistry studies have looked at leave-in conditioners as one of several hair products. In the Black Women's Health Study, which followed 50,543 women from 1997 to 2017 (2,311 incident breast cancers), the authors reported no association between conditioner use and breast cancer; heavy use of lye-containing relaxers was linked to a higher but not definitive risk of estrogen-receptor-positive cancer.[4] A New York survey of 301 women found that African-American and African-Caribbean women used more hair products, including leave-in conditioners, and more often used products containing placenta or endocrine-disrupting chemicals.[5] A preliminary gas-chromatography study of 18 hair products used by Black women, including leave-in conditioners, detected endocrine-disrupting or asthma-associated chemicals across product categories, with cyclosiloxanes, parabens and diethyl phthalate at the highest levels, and anti-frizz products containing cyclosiloxanes.[6] A 2026 study of 150 products marketed as clean for textured hair found that about 70 percent listed fragrance.[3]

A 2020 study of 1,558 Black women found that weekly leave-in conditioner use at age 10 was not associated with physical activity at that age, while research on hair maintenance as a barrier to exercise continues.[7] A 2026 laboratory study found that leave-in and co-wash conditioners had no antiviral activity against a surrogate virus in suspension tests, a finding relevant to shower-out biocontainment practice rather than appearance.[8]
No studies found. No human trials of leave-in conditioners as a product category were located.[2]
Related research consists of ingredient-level laboratory studies of conditioning agents on hair fibres, and observational studies of hair product use in different populations.[2][3][4][5]
